cls: Lubricant / emollient laxative (non-absorbed mineral hydrocarbon oil)
pharm: A highly refined, chemically inert mixture of saturated mineral hydrocarbons that is minimally absorbed and works mechanically by coating the bowel mucosa and faecal mass with an oily film, softening and lubricating stool to ease its passage.

summary: Liquid paraffin (mineral oil; paraffinum liquidum) is a highly refined, chemically inert mixture of saturated mineral hydrocarbons used orally as a lubricant/emollient laxative for occasional constipation and rectally (enema) for stool softening and faecal impaction. It is not significantly absorbed and works mechanically by coating the bowel mucosa and the faecal mass with an oily film, retarding colonic water reabsorption and softening and lubricating stool, typically producing a bowel movement within 6-8 hours. Its principal hazards are lipoid (exogenous) pneumonia from aspiration - so it is avoided in the very young, elderly, bedridden, and those with swallowing or neurological disorders - and, with prolonged use, malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and anal seepage with pruritus ani. It should be used occasionally and short-term (no more than about one week without medical advice), and has largely been superseded by osmotic and stimulant laxatives in modern guidelines.
indications: Stool softening and relief of faecal impaction (rectal enema)
Constipation in older children within product age limits

dosage.d: 15 mL as a single dose; maximum 45 mL/day
dosage.n: Onset 6-8 hours; short-term use only (US label: take at bedtime)

Take upright and well before lying down or bedtime in patients at risk of aspiration (EU guidance); the US OTC label conversely directs bedtime dosing - prefer the conservative approach in high-risk patients

moa: Liquid paraffin is a non-digestible, minimally absorbed mineral hydrocarbon oil. After oral administration it distributes through the intestinal lumen and coats the mucosal surface and the faecal bolus with a continuous oily film. This film lubricates stool passage and physically impedes reabsorption of water across the colonic wall, so the faecal mass retains water, stays soft and bulky, and is propelled more easily. It exerts no chemical, stimulant, or osmotic action and is essentially not absorbed systemically. The same non-absorbable oily nature drives its adverse effects: it traps co-ingested fat-soluble vitamins, and if aspirated it is engulfed by alveolar macrophages, producing chronic alveolar and interstitial inflammation (lipoid pneumonia).

absolute: Neurological or swallowing disorders predisposing to aspiration; drowsy, bedridden, or debilitated patients
Children below the product age limit (commonly under 6 years; some products contraindicate younger or all children)
Concurrent use of a stool softener (e.g., docusate)
relative: Undiagnosed abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting; suspected intestinal obstruction, appendicitis, diverticulitis, or ulcerative colitis
Use for more than one week
monitor: Fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) status with prolonged use

preg: Use should be limited; US labels advise pregnant women not to use without medical advice, and EU labels caution that prolonged use can cause maternal vitamin K malabsorption leading to neonatal hypoprothrombinemia and bleeding. Avoid prolonged use in pregnancy.
lact: Considered probably compatible with breastfeeding because infant exposure is minimal owing to negligible maternal absorption of the appropriate-molecular-weight oil. Topical paraffin breast creams should be avoided as they raise paraffin levels in milk.
renal: No dose adjustment is specified in labeling; systemic absorption is negligible.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is specified in labeling; systemic absorption is negligible.

major: Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K - reduced absorption with prolonged use
Warfarin and oral anticoagulants - vitamin K depletion may enhance anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
Docusate and other stool softeners - increase systemic absorption of mineral oil (granuloma risk); avoid combining
moderate: Other oral and fat-soluble drugs may have reduced absorption - separate dosing; oral contraceptive absorption may theoretically be reduced
interactions.food: Taking with meals reduces absorption of dietary fat-soluble vitamins - take between meals on an empty stomach.
interactions.diagnostics: Prolonged use may lower fat-soluble vitamin levels and raise INR; no specific assay interference.

common: Anal seepage with perianal irritation / pruritus ani
Nausea (especially with prolonged or excessive use)
serious: Fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency with chronic use, including vitamin-K-related coagulopathy
emergency: Respiratory symptoms (cough, breathlessness, fever) after dosing - suspect aspiration pneumonia
Rectal bleeding or failure to pass stool after use

monitoring: Fat-soluble vitamin status with prolonged use
Respiratory signs of aspiration in at-risk patients
counsel: Use only occasionally and for short periods (no more than about a week)

pearls: A lubricant, not a stimulant or osmotic laxative - it causes no cramping mechanism but is slow and messy (anal seepage)
Aspiration is the headline safety issue: avoid in the very young, elderly, bedridden, dysphagic, and neurologically impaired, and do not give at bedtime to high-risk patients
Do not co-prescribe with docusate (increases mineral-oil absorption and granuloma risk)
Chronic use causes silent fat-soluble vitamin deficiency - vitamin K depletion can raise INR and, in pregnancy, cause neonatal bleeding
Largely superseded by PEG, lactulose, and bisacodyl in modern constipation guidelines
missed: This is an as-needed laxative with no fixed schedule. Take it only when needed; do not take a double dose and do not exceed the maximum daily amount (45 mL for adults on the US OTC label).
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Excess causes oily diarrhea and anal seepage, cramping, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, and greater vitamin malabsorption; aspiration can cause lipoid pneumonia. Management is supportive: stop the drug, give symptomatic care and rehydration, monitor for aspiration, and consider vitamin supplementation after chronic excess.
